name: Orlen Hi-Vis Reflective Work Jacket
description:
A fluorescent yellow safety jacket with retro-reflective silver tape in a standard X-pattern across the chest and back. Two-tone construction — the body is a bright PVC-coated polyester, the sleeves are a slightly softer polyester for range of motion. Snap front closure, two lower patch pockets, one chest pocket. Meets city infrastructure visibility standards, which means if you work on roads, transit lines, utility corridors, or construction sites, you're probably required to own one.

This jacket doesn't pretend to be anything other than what it is. It's worn by the people who keep the city running at all hours. You see the yellow glow under elevated transit lines at 3am, in utility tunnels, in the rain. the Gray Zone has its own underground economy in these — expired or out-of-spec jackets that still look official enough to move through certain checkpoints without scrutiny.
what_it_says: You do physical work that the city depends on, often in conditions that would make other people call in sick.
worn_by: the Gray Zone residents using them as unofficial city worker disguises
anyone who needs to look official in a dimly lit corridor
story_hooks: A group of the Gray Zone residents wearing Orlen Hi-Vis jackets has been accessing restricted utility tunnels — they're not stealing anything, which makes it more confusing, not less.
The city infrastructure contract for Hi-Vis jackets was recently awarded to Orlen over a the Gray Zone cooperative that had held it for twenty years — the cooperative is not accepting this quietly.
Someone has been leaving messages on the back of Hi-Vis jackets abandoned in transit tunnels — written in a coded shorthand used by pre-2150 labor organizers.

physical_description.visual_profile: High-visibility safety jacket with commanding presence — bright fluorescent yellow demands attention. Utilitarian silhouette with squared shoulders, functional geometry, and authoritative reflective X-stripe pattern. Projects working-class infrastructure presence; worn by those maintaining GLMZ systems in darkness.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed, purposefully oversized for layering over thermal wear or light augmentation rigs. Allows freedom of movement for manual labor. Sleeves intentionally looser than torso for arm mobility during utility work.
physical_description.primary_material: Two-tone construction: PVC-coated polyester body (rigid, weather-resistant); softer polyester sleeves (flexible, less restrictive)
physical_description.texture: Stiff, protective sheen on torso panels; slightly matte, breathable weave on sleeves. Reflective tape has raised, bumped surface that catches light at all angles. Tactile industrial quality.
physical_description.color_scheme: Safety fluorescent yellow (#FFFF00) dominating entire garment. Silver-gray 3M retro-reflective tape in standard X-pattern across chest and back. Minimal color variation — purity of visibility is the design goal.
physical_description.closures: Snap-front closure (durable, operable with heavy gloves or augmented fingers). Two lower patch pockets with snap tabs; one chest pocket with snap closure.
distinctive_features: Retro-reflective X-stripe pattern meeting city infrastructure visibility codes
Two-tone material engineering — rigid body, flexible sleeves
Multiple functional pockets with industrial snaps
Orlen Safety Products branding (small, practical placement on sleeve)
Lightweight despite durability — designed for extended wear during night shifts
No fashion concessions — pure function aesthetic
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3 working-class, infrastructure essential tier. Signals honest labor maintaining city systems. Not aspirational; mandatory professional wear.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by transit workers, utility corridor maintainers, road construction crews, underground infrastructure teams, night-shift grid operators. Seen under elevated lines at 3am, in flooded tunnels, during grid storms. The jacket makes the worker visible to autonomous Behemoth traffic and drones. On the Gray Zone, expired jackets remain in circulation — worn as unofficial checkpoint passes or identity camouflage.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in quickly. Reflective tape edges fray slightly with age; PVC body develops creasing patterns from repetitive movement. Rain-stained hem. Faint mud-spray marks on lower panels. Still functional and regulation-compliant despite visible wear. Torn seams sometimes field-taped rather than replaced.
